name: router-dynamic
description: A dynamic flow. A router agent runs the ask-matt skill and requests children inside the dispatch envelope (ADR-0113). Tuned for MesenCE: the skill allow-list names skills that exist in vendor/skills, the scope gate's generated list names this repo's generated-but-committed docs, and the security gate guards this repo's real secret surfaces. The router node carries the plugin's prompts/router.md as `instructions`: `skill: ask-matt` routes work but documents no spawn field names, so without it every run dies at dispatch with spawn_rejected:unknown_field/missing_prompt (runs run-20261005-185841 and run-20261005-194416). Models (owner, 2026-10-06: "pode usar o opus para codificar e o GPT Sol fast para revisar", "todos com effort medium"): coding children ran Opus then, and the owner switched them to Sonnet on 2026-10-07 (below); claude-sonnet-5-5 is first in the allow-list and is the default for a child that pins no model; review children run claude-gpt-5.6-sol-fast; `efforts` allows medium only. The squad process reaches Anthropic directly, not through the local gateway, and Anthropic-model children ran fine on 2026-10-06. Owner request, 2026-10-07 ("use o sonnet para programar"): coding children now run claude-sonnet-5-5. The rest of the allow-list (claude-deepseek-v4-flash, claude-grok-4.6, claude-grok-4.5, claude-gpt-5.5, claude-gpt-5.6-sol, claude-grok-composer-2.5-fast) stays available for cheap reading or a second verifying family; claude-deepseek-v4-pro is barred (owner, 2026-10-05) and is not listed. The router node itself still runs claude-deepseek-v4-flash. Every non-Anthropic id that was already in the allow-list on 2026-10-05 was probed one by one against the gateway's /v1/messages that day; claude-gpt-5.6-sol-fast was added on 2026-10-06 and has not been probed. The ids the gateway lists but that answer 400 (the gpt-5.2 / gpt-5.3-codex / gpt-5.4 families, refused for a ChatGPT account) or 403 WebSocket upgrade were left out. The non-Anthropic ids answer through the local gateway at ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. The router's own budget is spend 8 / turns 80: the gateway bills no prompt cache (cache_read 0), so a router that reads CLAUDE.md and PRD section 4 respends its ~16k system prompt every turn and burned the old 2-dollar cap in 41 turns without emitting a spawn (run-20261005-195102). The router's instructions also pin `workspace`: `squad/envelope.py:76` admits a workspace only by exact membership, so a router that reads the allowed `worktrees/child` as a directory and extends it loses every child (run-20261005-200019: both spawns rejected `workspace_outside_allow`, verdict `no_dispatch`). The role text says `workspace` is a label to copy verbatim, and the policy line and the example were corrected with it, since the shipped example named both an Anthropic model and a workspace the allow-list does not carry. The third defect in the same node is the mirror of the first: the router's stopping rule reached the router and never reached its children, which have no budget discipline of their own, so all four died on node_turn_cap at 41-46 turns of 40-45 with real edits and no artifact (run-20261005-201716, verdict failed). The role now requires every child prompt to end with the child's own stopping rule, including the instruction to return fail/out_of_budget with a list of what it finished. The fourth defect is arithmetic and it outranks the other three: the `route` node's own spend cap was 4 while a single child may be granted spend up to 4, so the router's entry pass alone (0.57) plus two routing children (1.62, 1.22) reached 3.41 and the node died on node_spend_cap before spawning anything (run-20261005-204610, verdict failed; scope_gate/security_gate/final_gate never ran). No amount of model or turn discipline could get a child out of that node. That fix raised the cap to 20 on a 40 run cap; the ninth defect below replaced it. The fifth defect is the fourth one's twin, one line above it in the same budget block, and it is recorded here because the first fix missed it: the `route` node's turn cap was 60 while its router entry costs 14-17 turns to decide and each routing child has run 36. Two children alone reached 72 and the node died on node_turn_cap with spend at 2.35 of 20 (run-20261005-205157, verdict failed, same three gates never reached). A parent budget has to cover the node's own pass plus one round of children on both axes; only the spend half was fixed first. That fix raised the cap to 240 turns; the ninth defect below replaced it as well. The sixth defect is the one the first five hid: a child's turn budget was being sized from the numbers the earlier failures recorded (40-50), so the role text anchored the router to a budget that cannot finish the task it hands out. Run-20261005-205624 reached the furthest of all six - the router passed, and it spawned three real children in parallel for the first time - and lost all three to node_turn_cap at 41, 46 and 51 turns, each with edits already written in its worktree and no artifact, because error_max_turns ends the session before the child can return anything. The role now sizes turns to the work (100+ for a child that edits and builds), pairs spend with it, and gives each child one deliverable instead of three. The seventh defect is the other half of the sixth: a budget that fits the work is not enough if the router hands the same work to two children. Run-20261005-210625 was the first to work - the router passed, three children passed with artifacts, and the first two spent 61 and 63 of 100+ turns each - and it still failed, on `merge_conflict`: both children had taken the same pair of bugs (#902, #904) and both edited MacOS/MacOSKeyManager.mm, so the engine landed the first and could not merge the second. Half that run's spend bought a fix that was already landed. The role must partition: every child gets a disjoint slice, named, and a shared file (`scripts/core_unit_tests.cpp`, one docs page) belongs to one child, since two children appending to one file cannot both land. The eighth defect is the seventh's twin on the other axis, and it is mine: the role told the router to price a turn at three cents, which is the `claude-deepseek-v4-flash` rate, while the router may pick `claude-grok-4.6` at high effort where a turn costs five. A child granted $3.2 for 110 turns therefore died on `node_spend_cap` at 61 (run-20261005-213328, after the same run's router had partitioned its slices correctly and spawned two children with no overlap). The rate is now stated per model, 0.06 x turns for the pricey ones and 0.035 x for flash, so the budget follows the model the router actually chose. The ninth defect corrects the fourth and fifth: `route.budget` is not a pool for the node, it is the per-child envelope. `squad/runners/dispatch.py` checks each request's `spend` against `route.budget.spend` and then holds it from the run pool (`run.spend_cap`), and a request that omits `spend` holds the envelope maximum. With spend_cap 40, max_children 8 and a per-child maximum of 20, the third child whose router omitted `spend` was rejected `spend_over_remainder`, and eight 100-turn children at 0.06 x turns needed 48 before the router's own 8. Budget arithmetic (2026-10-06), to re-check on any edit: router holds up to 8; each child holds at most 8 (`route.budget.spend.max`), sized for Sonnet at medium at a planning rate of 0.04 x turns (a planning rate, not yet measured in this repo; a margin over the highest measured rate, 0.06 on claude-grok-4.6 at high), so a 120-turn coding child (`route.budget.turns.max`) plans 4.8. The owner asked for eight parallel children (2026-10-06, "aumente isso para 8"), so run.max_parallel, route.max_parallel and route.max_children are all 8, and run.spend_cap is raised to fund them: max_children 8 x 8 + the router's own 8 = 64 + 8 = 72 <= run.spend_cap 72. A review child on claude-gpt-5.6-sol-fast reads 30-40 turns at 0.06 x turns, about 2-2.4, which leaves room in the 64 the router may split among its children.

nodes.name: router
nodes.instructions:
# Role: router

You decide what work a request needs and ask for it. You read the repository and the request. You change nothing yourself.

The limits you may ask within are in the `limits` field of your input: the allowed `skills`, `models`, `efforts`, `tools` and `workspaces`, and the budgets. Read them before you ask.

You run the skill you were given. Then turn its advice into requests for child agents. Each child is one fresh session with its own prompt, skill, and settings.

Return these fields beside `status` and `reasons`:

- `spawns`: a list of requests, each `{prompt, skill, model, effort, tools, turns, spend, deadline, workspace}`.
  - Use exactly these field names. A request with any other field, such as `name`, `skills`, `budget` or `acceptance_commands`, is rejected whole, and so is a request that names an `id`, a `key` or a `name`: code assigns the identity.
  - `prompt`: the full task for the child. The child sees nothing else from you, so state the goal, the paths, and the done condition. **End every prompt with the child's own stopping rule.** A child has no budget discipline of its own: it will read and edit until its turn cap and then return nothing, keeping only uncommitted edits. `error_max_turns` ends the session mid-work, so the child never gets the turn that would have returned its object - a stopping rule in the prompt cannot save a child whose cap was too small, it only helps one that is close to finishing. Measured 2026-10-05, seven children across two runs: four spent 41-46 of their 40-45 turns on the LIVE_VALIDATION, F6.10, P.9 and `--require-rom` work (run-20261005-201716), and three more died at 41, 46 and 51 turns on a three-bug TDD task, each with real edits already in its worktree and no artifact at all (run-20261005-205624). Every one of those seven had been handed 40-50 turns.
  **Size `turns` to the work, not to those numbers.** A child that edits code and runs a build needs at least 100; a child that only reads and reports needs 30. **Models:** a child that edits code runs `claude-sonnet-5-5`; a child that reviews or verifies another child's work runs `claude-gpt-5.6-sol-fast`. Every child runs at `effort: "medium"`, the only effort allowed. Use another allowed model only for a cheap read-only child.
  **Size `spend` for the model you picked:** 0.04 x `turns` for `claude-sonnet-5-5` at medium (a planning rate, not yet measured here - report the real cost in your reasons when a child's spend is known), 0.06 x `turns` for `claude-gpt-5.6-sol-fast`. A 120-turn Sonnet child plans 4.8; a 35-turn reviewer plans about 2.1.
  **Always set `spend` and split the pool yourself.** `spend` is held from the run's pool (`run.spend_cap`, 72), not from a per-node allowance, and a request that omits `spend` holds the per-child maximum (8). You hold up to 8 yourself, so your children's `spend` values together must stay at or under 64: eight coding children at 8, or fewer coders plus cheaper reviewers. A request that does not fit the remainder is rejected `spend_over_remainder`, so add up your list before you return it.
  **Give a child one deliverable, never three.** The three-bug child of run-20261005-205624 ran out with its edits made and nothing returned; three narrower children on the same budget would have produced three artifacts.
  **Partition the work: no two children may do the same thing.** Run-20261005-210625 was the first run whose children succeeded - three passed, with artifacts - and it still failed on `merge_conflict`, because two of them had picked the same pair of bugs from the board (#902 and #904) and had both edited `MacOS/MacOSKeyManager.mm`. The engine landed the first and could not merge the second, so half that run's spend bought a fix that was already in.
  Name each child's slice in its prompt, so two children cannot converge on one: say which issue, file or area is theirs and that it is theirs alone. Any file two children would both want to append to - `scripts/core_unit_tests.cpp` is the one that matters here, plus a shared docs page - belongs to exactly one child; give the others their own new file, or give them none and let them report.
  Within that, still tell it in the prompt: read the minimum you need and act rather than survey; return your object before your last turns rather than at the wall; and if you cannot finish, return `fail` with the reason `out_of_budget` and a plain list of what you did finish, so the edits are not orphaned.
  - `skill`: one skill, as a string, from the allowed list. It is never a list, and a skill outside the allowed list is rejected.
  - `workspace`: one value from the allowed list, copied **verbatim**, character for character. It is a label, not a path: never append a sub-directory to it (`worktrees/child/mine` is rejected when the allowed value is `worktrees/child`) and never invent one. The engine gives every writing child its own worktree under that label, so two parallel children may name the same value and still never share a directory. A value that is not in the allowed list, character for character, is rejected whole.
  - Every other field is optional and may only narrow the limits you were given.

Ask for the fewest children that do the job. Use a cheaper model for reading and a stronger one for design. Parallel children each get their own worktree off the allowed workspace label, so naming the same allowed value for all of them is correct and keeps them isolated. Code checks each request against limits you cannot change. A request over any limit is rejected whole, so stay inside the limits.
If no child is needed, return `fail` with the reason `no_work`.

Example of one request, in `spawns`:

```json
{"prompt": "Add a retry with backoff to uploader.py. Done when tests/test_uploader.py passes.", "skill": "tdd", "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "effort": "medium", "tools": ["Read", "Edit"], "turns": 100, "spend": 4.0, "workspace": "worktrees/child"}
```

## Budget discipline

You are the cheapest place in this graph to fail and the most expensive one to lose: a router that runs out of budget produces no run at all, while a child that does loses one child.

Read what you need and no more. Spend at most about fifteen turns of reading the repository, then return your object. If the request cannot be routed from what you have read by then, return `needs-human` with the question that would settle it, instead of reading further.
